title: TB8-13041
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I dismiss the appeal brought by XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of Iran.

The Appellant alleges that he is a follower of the Gonabadi Dervish faith and fears persecution because the Iranian government is against his faith. He alleges that he was detained due to his faith in 2011 and 2014. He arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017 to visit family. He alleges that he filed a refugee claim after his wife told him on November 9, 2017 that Iranian authorities were looking for him.

The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that the Appellant's allegations were not credibly established, on a balance of probabilities. The RPD found that key aspects of the Appellant's evidence about his faith were inconsistent with the objective documents, that his evidence about his arrests was inconsistent, and that he had not presented corroborating documents which were reasonably available to him. The RPD also held that the Appellant lacked subjective fear.

The Appellant argues that the RPD's assessment of the Appellant's religious knowledge was narrow and microscopic. He further argues that he was consistent about his detentions and gave a reasonable explanation for subjective fear concerns. Finally, he argues that the RPD failed to assess his evidence under section 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). He submits one piece of new evidence on appeal.
I find that the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant had not credibly established his allegations, on a balance of probabilities.
I confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

According to the law,1 I can only accept evidence that: (i) arose after the RPD's decision; or (ii) was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or (iii) that could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.2

The Appellant submitted one new piece of evidence, a newspaper article about the execution of a Dervish follower.3 The article details events which post date the rejection of the claim. Therefore, it meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA and is new, pursuant to the case law. It comes from Amnesty International and is therefore credible. It is relevant to the appeal because it deals with the treatment of Dervishes in Iran. I therefore admit it.

The article does not meet the test for an oral hearing as it does not raise any credibility issues related to the Appellant. The Appellant did not request an oral hearing. THE ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION (RAD)

My role is to look at all of the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.4 There is an exception to this, where the RAD defers to the RPD if the RPD had a meaningful advantage in assessing the credibility of oral evidence. I do not find this case falls into the exception. Therefore, I will be looking at whether the RPD's decision was correct.

The RPD found that the Appellant had not established he was a genuine follower of the Gonabadi Dervish faith. I concur with the RPD. I will address the issues as follows. (a) The RPD correctly assessed the Appellant's religious profile; (b) The RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant was inconsistent about his detentions; (c) The Appellant failed to provide relevant corroborating documents; (d) The RPD correctly concluded the Appellant lacked subjective fear; and (e) The RPD did not fail to evaluate the claim under sections 96 and 97. The RPD correctly assessed the Appellant's religious profile

The RPD held that the Appellant had not established he was a genuine Dervish practitioner because he was unable to explain the central ideology of the faith and important components of its ceremonies.5 The Appellant argues that this was an error because the RPD failed to consider the totality of the Appellant's testimony on his faith and was too narrow and microscopic in its focus.6 The Appellant argues that his testimony was scattered as opposed to vague, as the RPD found. I concur with the RPD.

I do not find the Appellant's testimony was scattered, in the sense that it was given at various locations but can be put together to form a coherent and credible narrative. Rather, listening to the recording in its totality, I find the testimony to be vague, in that the Appellant was uncertain and unclear in many of his answers. I, therefore, do not find the RPD mischaracterized the Appellant's testimony.

Further, the Appellant does not challenge the RPD's finding that the Appellant gave inconsistent testimony on the three core beliefs of the Dervish faith and about the importance of music in Dervish ceremonies. Reviewing the record, I see no error in these findings. Rather, the Appellant argues that these conclusions took too narrow of a focus, and the Appellant's testimony on the whole was credible. I do not find this persuasive. First, the issues that the RPD considered are central to the beliefs and practice of the Appellant. Given the Appellant's evidence that he had been a practicing Dervish since 2009,7 it was correct that the RPD expected the Appellant to give consistent testimony on this point. The Appellant did not need to testify using the exact language of the Immigration and Refugee Board's (Board's) Response to Information Request (RIR), but it was not an error to expect him to recall the broad concepts contained therein, and he did not do so. Moreover, the RPD did not place undue weight on these issues, because they are central to the faith.

Further, the Appellant asserts that the remainder of his testimony about his faith was credible, and the RPD was obligated to consider all of the testimony as a whole. I have reviewed the transcript of the RPD hearing, and I do not agree. As the Appellant argues, he did give some testimony which was consistent with objective evidence on the Dervish faith. However, I do not concur with the Appellant that his testimony, looked at as a whole, was credible.

For example, the Appellant gave inconsistent testimony about where the Dervish faith was located within the larger religious structure. He was asked about whether the Gonabadi Dervish faith was a branch of a larger religion, and he stated that it is a way of looking at Islam.8 The RPD then asked if the Appellant was familiar with the Nimatullahi Sufi Order, and he stated that he was. He was asked how many branches there were, and he stated there was one: the Dervish Gonabadi. The RPD put to the Appellant that this was inconsistent with the Board's documentation stating that the Gonabadi order is one of the three main branches of the Nimatullahi Sufi order.9 The Appellant then stated that there are other branches. In my view, this is not a reasonable explanation, as it does not explain why the Appellant initially stated there is one branch in the Nimatullahi Sufi Order. This is not, as the Appellant argues, a clarification, as it occurred only once the RPD pointed out that the Appellant's initial answer was incorrect.10 The Appellant alleges that his testimony on the whole was credible, but I find this to be yet another example of the lack of credibility in his testimony.

I acknowledge that the Appellant gave some testimony which was consistent with the Board's documentation on the Dervish faith. However, when I consider the testimony in its totality, I find that the credibility concerns discussed above constitute significant issues with important aspects of the Appellant's testimony. Therefore, I see no error in the RPD's decision. Moreover, I note that the RPD's assessment is consistent with the Federal Court's guidance on assessing religious belief in a refugee claim. The Federal Court has stated that, while the Board is not permitted to engage in a test of religious trivia or base the conclusions on an assessment of "theological soundness", the Board can engage in religious questioning where the Board considers "whether the claimant holds a level of religious knowledge that would be expected of someone in the claimant's position."11

I find that the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant did not hold a level of religious knowledge of someone who had been regularly practicing the Dervish faith since 2009, which was nine years before the RPD hearing. I therefore find that the RPD correctly considered the evidence about the Appellant's religious practices. The RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant was inconsistent about his detentions

The RPD held that the Appellant was inconsistent in his evidence about when he had been detained on the basis of his faith, and it drew a negative inference as to his credibility on this basis.12 The Appellant argues that the Appellant was consistent and provided an explanation for this issue and that the issue is minor.13 I do not find this argument to be persuasive.

The Appellant gave numerous different accounts of his interactions with Iranian authorities. For ease of reference, I have summarized the contradictory evidence in a chart. Schedule A14 Arrested on XXXX XXXX, 2011 and detained for five days. Schedule 1215 Detained from XXXX XXXX, 2011 to XXXX XXXX, 2017. Arrested and detained. BOC16 Detained for five nights on XXXX XXXX, 2014. Testimony17 Arrested once on XXXX XXXX, 2014. Testimony18 Mere detention, once in 2011. Testimony19 Arrested once for five days in 2011 and detained once in 2014. Post-hearing affidavit20 Translators note states there were two dates of detention and errors are the fault of the translator.

The Appellant argues that this evidence is consistent and is explained by the post-hearing evidence of a translator who stated that the mistakes in the written documents were due to his own error. The RPD considered all of this evidence and the explanations for the inconsistencies and found them to be unreasonable for several reasons: (a) The Appellant contradicted himself in testimony as to which was the mere detention and which was the arrest as between the 2011 and 2014 incidents; (b) The Appellant failed to clearly answer why he had changed his testimony; (c) The Appellant testified that his problems started in 2014, and when asked why he did not say 2011, he said that the five-night detention did not bother him, which the RPD found not to be logical; and (d) The testimony on this point evolved, and the Appellant was evasive.

Reviewing the record, I agree with this. While I have summarized the testimony here, reviewing it, it is apparent that the Appellant is changing his testimony as the inconsistencies are put to him. If the inconsistency was truly from a translator's error, then I would expect the Appellant to have initially stated that he was apprehended twice. Further, the Appellant wishes to rely on the translator's affidavit and the use of the Gregorian calendar to absolve him of the inconsistencies, but I do not find this reasonable. The Appellant had the assistance of Counsel in preparing his Schedule A, Schedule 12 and Basis of Claim (BOC) forms.21 He declared that the BOC had been interpreted to him.22 Accordingly, I do not find it was reasonable that he did not list both detentions in his forms. At a minimum, even if there was an issue with converting the dates to the Gregorian calendar, the Appellant could have seen that only one date was listed and only one arrest described in each form. The BOC narrative describes only one incident as well. The Appellant signed the declaration that this was interpreted to him. I would expect that he would be able to notice that only one detention was described, even if he was not clear on the date. Moreover, I find it concerning that the translator states that he reviewed his notes but did not provide them as evidence.23 Therefore, I do not find the RPD erred in concluding that the evidence on this point was inconsistent.

Finally, I do not accept the inconsistency to be minor or insignificant, as the Appellant argues. The Appellant's entire claim is based on his risk of mistreatment based on being Dervish. Whether he was previously mistreated for this reason is highly relevant to his future risk. The inconsistencies here are significant. For these reasons, I find the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant was inconsistent about his detentions. I find that, based upon this, the Appellant has not established that these detentions occurred, on a balance of probabilities. The Appellant failed to provide relevant corroborating documents

The RPD held that the Appellant failed to make efforts to obtain reasonably available corroborative evidence, including evidence of injuries he allegedly sustained at the hands of Iranian authorities, letters from his wife and family, letters from the families of his Dervish friends who were imprisoned. The RPD held that the Appellant's evidence was that he began meeting with his lawyer on December 1, 2017, and the hearing was on April 12, 2018, which gave the Appellant sufficient time to attempt to obtain evidence and that the Appellant's explanation that he never thought of getting such documents because his initial plan was not to stay in Canada was not reasonable given the length of time and the fact that the Appellant had Counsel.24

The Appellant has not challenged this finding, and reviewing the record, I concur with it. While there is case law suggesting that a lack of corroborating documents alone is not reason to reject a claim, where the testimony is otherwise credible, here the RPD found credibility concerns, which I am confirming. Moreover, the documentation which the RPD considered could have addressed some of the concerns that the RPD raised. For example, the Appellant alleged he had lasting XXXX XXXX from his detention, and he had received medical attention for this but did not think to provide the documentary proof. This evidence relates to the credibility of the detention, which was in issue before the RPD.

Moreover, what is central to the finding in this regard is the Appellant's lack of efforts to get documents and his failure to provide reasonable explanations. I concur with the RPD that the Appellant had Counsel and time to obtain documents and failed to make reasonable efforts. For these reasons, I concur with the RPD that the failure to provide a reasonable explanation for obtaining corroborating documents undermines the credibility of the Appellant's allegations. The RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant lacked subjective fear

The RPD considered the Appellant's delay in leaving Iran permanently, his failure to claim protection elsewhere, his re-availment to Iran and his delay in making a claim in Canada, and it found that there were concerns in this regard but found that this was not determinative based on the credibility concerns.25

The Appellant argues that he gave a reasonable explanation for these issues, specifically that he loved his country and did not plan to make a claim until his wife told him that the Sepah had come to his home and looked for him.26 I concur with the RPD.

I acknowledge that the Appellant alleged that he loved Iran and did not plan to leave permanently until the 2017 incident and that he took steps to mitigate his risk after the 2014 arrest. However, given that the Appellant alleged two previous arrests or detentions, one of which he alleged resulted in permanent injury, and given he had an extensive travel history including at least two trips to France which postdated these detentions,27 I do not find the explanation to be reasonable. I therefore reject the Appellant's argument on this.

Ultimately, this issue is not determinative, as I agree with the RPD that the credibility concerns discussed above are determinative. The RPD did not fail to evaluate the claim under sections 96 and 97

The Appellant argues that the RPD failed to assess the Appellant's claim under sections 96 and 97 and that, despite the credibility findings, the Member had the "responsibility of determining on all the un-impugned evidence whether the claimant is a refugee."28 This argument does not apply in this case.

There may be cases where negative credibility findings are not determinative, but this is not one of those cases. There is no un-impugned evidence. The RPD did not accept that the Appellant had established he was Dervish or had been previously arrested, on a balance of probabilities. There was nothing left to be evaluated against section 96 or 97 of the IRPA. The Appellant goes on to argue that there is ample evidence of the persecution of Dervishes in Iran, but this fails to consider that the RPD held that the Appellant had not established he was a Dervish.
For these reasons, this argument fails.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.
